name: fasting

attributes.attribute: Celtic ritual, troscad in Irish and ymprydio in Welsh
tradition of protest in Ireland and Wales
only reprisal for a harmed person
honour price kings and bards could dodge

sources: Kelly, Fergus. A Guide to Early Irish Law. Vol. III. Dublin: School of Celtic Studies, Dublin Institute for Advanced Studies, Early Irish Law Series, 1988, 182+.
Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: Fasting, called troscad in Irish and ymprydio in Welsh, was a Celtic ritual. 'To fast against one's enemy' was a tradition of protest in Ireland and Wales. A victim of a wrong would sit on the doorstep of the wrongdoer. He took no food and told passersby of the crime. Kings and BARDS could dodge the ERIC, or honour price. For the harmed person, fasting stood as the only reprisal. The protest often worked and set matters right. Ancient mythological texts record it. The practice never vanished. It returned at times as a nonviolent form of protest.

okr.objective: Fasting against one's enemy was a Celtic ritual and form of protest.
key_results: Fasting served as a traditional protest in Ireland and Wales.
A victim sat on the doorstep of the wrongdoer, taking no food.
For a harmed person, fasting stood as the only reprisal.
The practice returned at times as nonviolent protest.
